Act 1 · The label problem

01ImageNet1.2 million images, years of human labelling

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 1 · The label problem · Day 3 · 08 / 105

3.08 · cards

Day 1 and Day 2 models all depend on someone labelling thousands of examples.

Act 1 · The label problem

The closed-set assumption

Closed-set assumption — a classifier assumes every input belongs to one of its training classes. It has no way to say "none of these".
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 1 · The label problem · Day 3 · 09 / 105

3.09 · definition

A 10-class model must answer one of 10, even for something it has never seen.

Worked example

Overconfidence on the unknown

  1. A cat-vs-dog classifier is shown a car
  2. softmax must sum to 1 → "dog 97%"
  3. High confidence does not mean the model knows
  4. It just means one class scored higher than the other
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 1 · The label problem · Day 3 · 10 / 105

3.10 · worked

Softmax confidence is not a measure of "I have seen something like this before".

Act 1 · The label problem

Out-of-distribution inputs

Out-of-distribution (OOD) — an input unlike anything in the training data: a new object, a new camera, night instead of day. Models often fail on these silently and confidently.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 1 · The label problem · Day 3 · 11 / 105

3.11 · definition

In production, OOD inputs arrive every day. The camera moves, the season changes.

Act 1 · The label problem

Two escape routes

Route 1

  • learn without labels
  • the data supervises itself (Act 3)

Route 2

  • learn from text
  • captions on the internet supervise vision (Act 4)
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 1 · The label problem · Day 3 · 12 / 105

3.12 · compare

Attention and the Vision Transformer

What if every part of the image could look at every other part?

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 14 / 105

3.14 · section

Climb starts here.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer

Recap: CNNs see locally

01A 3 × 3 kernel sees 9 pixels
02The view grows slowly with depth
03Two far-apart parts of an image only "meet" deep in the network
04Global context arrives late
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 15 / 105

3.15 · cards

This was the first limit we listed at the end of Day 1.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer

Attention in plain words

Attention — each part of the input looks at every other part, decides how relevant each one is, and builds its new meaning as a weighted mix of the relevant parts.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 16 / 105

3.16 · definition

Every part asks: who in this image matters to me?

Worked example

Attention with a sentence first

  1. "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired."
  2. What does "it" refer to?
  3. Attention puts high weight on "animal", low weight on "street"
  4. The meaning of "it" is built mostly from "animal"
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 17 / 105

3.17 · worked

Change "tired" to "wide" and the weight moves to "street". Context decides.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer

Attention in an image

  • A patch showing part of a wheel attends strongly to the patches showing the rest of the car
  • weakly to the sky
  • Its meaning becomes "car wheel", not just "round dark thing"
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 18 / 105

3.18 · diagram

One layer of attention gives every patch a global view.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer

Query, key, value

01Query"what am I looking for?"
02Key"what do I contain?" (a label on each part)
03Value"what information do I pass on?"
04Relevance = how well a query matches each key
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 19 / 105

3.19 · cards

Like searching a library: your question is the query, book titles are keys, book contents are values.

Worked example

Attention — tiny worked example

  1. Query q = (1, 0)
  2. Keys: k₁ = (1, 0), k₂ = (0, 1)
  3. Scores: q·k₁ = 1, q·k₂ = 0
  4. softmax → weights ≈ 0.73 and 0.27
  5. Output = 0.73 × v₁ + 0.27 × v₂
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 20 / 105

3.20 · worked

Dot product measures match, softmax turns the scores into weights, then we mix the values. That is all attention is.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Attention has no sense of order

Attention treats its input as a set. Shuffle the patches and attention gives the same result. So we add position information to every patch.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 21 / 105

3.21 · rule

This is called positional encoding. Without it, the model would not know top from bottom.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer

The Vision Transformer (ViT)

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 22 / 105

3.22 · diagram

An image is treated like a sentence, where each patch is a word.

Worked example

ViT — counting tokens

  1. Image 224 × 224
  2. patch 16 × 16
  3. 224 / 16 = 14 → 14 × 14 = 196 patches
  4. + 1 [CLS] token = 197 tokens
  5. each patch = 16 × 16 × 3 = 768 numbers
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 23 / 105

3.23 · worked

Attention compares every token with every other token: about 197 squared, roughly 39,000 pairs per layer. That cost grows fast with resolution.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer

The [CLS] token

[CLS] token — an extra learned token added to the sequence. Through attention it gathers information from all patches, and its final value is used for classification.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 24 / 105

3.24 · definition

It is like a reporter that listens to every patch and writes the summary.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer

CNN vs ViT

Built-in assumptionsCNN: locality and shift-tolerance built inViT: almost none — learns them
Data neededCNN: works on moderate dataViT: needs huge data or pretraining
Global contextCNN: lateViT: from the first layer
Cost with resolutionCNN: grows linearlyViT: grows with tokens squared
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 25 / 105

3.25 · table

CNNs come with good instincts. ViTs must learn them, which needs a lot of data. That is why self-supervision matters for ViTs.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · When ViT wins

Small data → CNNs usually win. Huge data or a strong pretrained model → ViTs match or beat them and transfer extremely well.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 26 / 105

3.26 · rule

In practice you rarely train a ViT from scratch. You use a pretrained one.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer

DETR revisited

01Yesterday
02DETR uses "object queries" and needs no NMS
03Today you can read it
04object queries are queries in attention
05each one attends to the image and claims one object
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 27 / 105

3.27 · cards

Yesterday's mystery box now makes sense.

Act 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer

The family grows

01Swin Transformerattention inside local windows, shifted each layer · cheaper, hierarchical like a CNN
02ConvNeXta CNN modernised with transformer design choices · "the CNN strikes back"
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Attention and the Vision Transformer · Day 3 · 28 / 105

3.28 · cards

(cut first) The two families borrow from each other. Neither won outright.

Act 3 · Learning without labels

Self-supervised learning

Self-supervised learning — training on a task created automatically from the data itself, so no human labels are needed. The real goal is the features the model learns along the way.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 30 / 105

3.30 · definition

We do not care about the made-up task. We care about what the network learns while solving it.

Act 3 · Learning without labels

Pretext tasks

01Colourisationpredict colours from a gray image
02Jigsawput shuffled patches back in order
03Rotationpredict how much the image was rotated
04Maskinghide patches, predict what was there
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 31 / 105

3.31 · cards

To colour a banana yellow, the model must first recognise a banana. That is the trick.

Act 3 · Learning without labels · Contrastive learning: the idea

Two different views of the same image should look similar to the model. Views of different images should look different.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 32 / 105

3.32 · rule

This simple rule trains some of the strongest vision models in existence.

Act 3 · Learning without labels

SimCLR — how it works

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 33 / 105

3.33 · diagram

Positive pair: two views of one image. Negatives: everything else. Day 1's augmentation becomes the teacher.

Act 3 · Learning without labels

Why augmentation is the teacher

01Cropteaches "part of a dog is still the dog"
02Colour changeteaches "colour is not identity"
03Blurteaches "fine texture is not identity"
04The model learns what stays the same under all of them: the object
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 34 / 105

3.34 · cards

Augmentation choice decides what the model learns to ignore.

Act 3 · Learning without labels

Embeddings

Embedding — a list of numbers (a vector) that represents an image's meaning. Similar images get vectors that are close together.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 35 / 105

3.35 · definition

Think of every image as a point on a map, where similar images sit near each other.

Worked example

Cosine similarity — worked

  1. a = (1, 2)
  2. b = (2, 4)
  3. c = (2, −1)
  4. cos(a, b) = 10 / (√5
  5. √20) = 1.0 → same direction
  6. cos(a, c) = 0 / (√5
  7. √5) = 0 → unrelated
  8. Range −1 to 1
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 36 / 105

3.36 · worked

Cosine similarity cares about direction, not length. It is how we compare embeddings everywhere today.

Act 3 · Learning without labels

DINO and DINOv2

01Self-supervised training on huge image collections
02Features so good that one frozen backbone works for many tasks
03Its attention separates objects from background without ever seeing a mask
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 37 / 105

3.37 · cards

Nobody told DINO what an object is. It discovered object boundaries on its own.

Act 3 · Learning without labels

One frozen backbone, many tasks

  • DINOv2 backbone (frozen) → small head → classification
  • small head → segmentation
  • small head → depth
  • nearest neighbours → image retrieval
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 38 / 105

3.38 · diagram

Train the expensive part once, reuse it everywhere. That is the foundation-model idea.

Act 3 · Learning without labels

What you can build on embeddings

01Image searchfind similar photos
02Duplicate detection
03Clusteringgroup a photo dump
04Few-shot classificationlabel 5 examples per class, use nearest neighbours
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 39 / 105

3.39 · cards

None of these need training a model. Lab 3A builds image search.

Worked example

Few-shot with nearest neighbours

  1. 5 labelled photos per class → embed them
  2. New photo → embed → find the 3 closest labelled embeddings
  3. 2 say "crack", 1 says "stain" → predict "crack"
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Learning without labels · Day 3 · 40 / 105

3.40 · worked

With good embeddings, five examples can be enough. Compare that with Day 1's 50,000 CIFAR images.

Act 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP · The idea behind CLIP

The internet already contains hundreds of millions of images with captions written by people. Use the captions as labels.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP · Day 3 · 42 / 105

3.42 · rule

No one labels anything new. The captions were already there.

Act 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP

CLIP

CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training) — two encoders, one for images and one for text, trained so that an image and its caption produce similar embeddings. Trained on about 400 million image–text pairs.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP · Day 3 · 43 / 105

3.43 · definition

Same contrastive idea as SimCLR, but the positive pair is an image and its caption.

Act 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP

Contrastive training as a matrix

  • A batch of N images and N captions → N × N similarity grid
  • Diagonal = correct image–caption pairs → push up
  • Everything else = wrong pairs → push down
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP · Day 3 · 44 / 105

3.44 · diagram

For a batch of 4 there are 16 scores: 4 right, 12 wrong. Real batches have tens of thousands of pairs.

Act 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP

A shared embedding space

  • Images and sentences live on the same map
  • photo of a dog ≈ "a photo of a dog"
  • photo of a palm tree ≈ "a palm tree in the desert"
  • Distance = how well they match
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP · Day 3 · 45 / 105

3.45 · diagram

Once text and images share a space, you can compare any image with any sentence.

Act 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP

Zero-shot classification

Zero-shot classification — classifying images into classes the model was never explicitly trained on, by describing the classes in words.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP · Day 3 · 46 / 105

3.46 · definition

Zero shots means zero training examples for your classes.

Worked example

Zero-shot — step by step

  1. Classes: cat, dog, car
  2. Write sentences: "a photo of a cat", "a photo of a dog", "a photo of a car"
  3. Embed the image and the 3 sentences
  4. Cosine similarities: 0.31, 0.24, 0.12
  5. Highest → "cat"
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP · Day 3 · 47 / 105

3.47 · worked

No training. To add a class, add a sentence. That is the power.

Act 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP

Prompt wording matters

"cat"

  • bare words often score worse

"a photo of a cat"

  • matches how captions are written

Prompt ensembling · average several templates ("a photo of a …", "a close-up of a …") · often a few points more accurate

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP · Day 3 · 48 / 105

3.48 · compare

CLIP learned from captions, so talk to it like a caption.

Act 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP

CLIP as infrastructure

01Image search by text
02Zero-shot classifiers
03The text encoder that steers image generators (Act 7)
04The vision encoder inside many vision-language models (Act 6)
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Connecting images and words: CLIP · Day 3 · 49 / 105

CLIP matches overall meaning, not precise structure.

01Typographic attackan apple with a paper label "iPod" → classified as an iPod

Closed vs open vocabulary

Closed vocabulary

  • a fixed list of classes chosen at training time
  • new class → new labels, retrain

Open vocabulary

  • classes given as text at run time
  • new class → type a new word

Open-vocabulary detection — a detector that takes text prompts and returns boxes for whatever the text describes, including classes it never saw in box-labelled training data.

Act 5 · Open vocabulary: detect and segment anything you can name

The trade-off

Foundation model, zero-shot

  • no labels, fast to start
  • slower, larger, less accurate on your specific case

Fine-tuned model

  • needs labels and training
  • smaller, faster, more accurate on your case

Common pattern: use the foundation model to label data, then fine-tune a small fast model

Worked example

Counting visual tokens — worked

  1. LLaVA-1.5
  2. vision encoder with 14 × 14 patches
  3. image 336 × 336
  4. 336 / 14 = 24 → 24 × 24 = 576 visual tokens
  5. Double the resolution → about 4× the tokens → slower and more expensive

The latent space

Latent space — the compressed space of codes inside a generative model. Nearby codes produce similar images; moving through it changes the image smoothly.

Act 7 · Machines that draw (Read at home)

Diffusion: the idea

  • Forward: add a little noise to an image, step by step, until it is pure noise
  • Reverse: train a network to remove a little noise at each step
  • Generate: start from pure noise and denoise step by step
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 7 · Machines that draw (Read at home) · Day 3 · 85 / 105

Destroying an image is easy. Learning to undo one small step of destruction is learnable.

Act 7 · Machines that draw (Read at home)

Latent diffusion (Stable Diffusion)

Pixel diffusion

  • denoise full-size images
  • very expensive

Latent diffusion

  • compress to a small latent first, denoise there, decode at the end
  • much cheaper, runs on a single GPU

Worked example

Quantisation

  1. FP32
  2. 4 bytes per weight → INT8
  3. 1 byte per weight
  4. Model 4× smaller and often 2–4× faster
  5. Small accuracy drop
  6. always re-measure after quantising

Close of the course

Day 3 recap

  • Classifiers are stuck with their classes and overconfident on the unknown
  • Attention lets every patch see every other patch
  • ViT turns an image into 197 tokens
  • Contrastive learning makes good embeddings without labels
  • CLIP puts images and text in one space → zero-shot
  • Grounding DINO + SAM: text → box → mask
  • Pick the tool from the problem, not the hype
